summary: This document defines the SVCB and HTTPS DNS record types, which tell clients how to reach a service before connecting. They can list multiple alternative endpoints with parameters such as transport settings, support future extensions like keys for encrypting the TLS ClientHello, and allow aliasing of a zone apex, which a CNAME cannot do.

eli5.summary: Before you visit a shop, a sign tells you which door is best, which languages they speak, and a different address if this one is closed. SVCB is that sign for websites.

subtitle: DNS records that tell a client how to reach a service, with protocols, ports and aliases, before it connects.

tldr.problem: Clients normally learn only IP addresses from A and AAAA records, so they cannot learn about HTTP/3, other ports or alternative endpoints before connecting, and a CNAME cannot be used at a zone apex.
tldr.mechanism: The SVCB record (type 64) and its HTTPS variant (type 65) carry a priority, a target name and extensible key=value parameters, in either AliasMode or ServiceMode.
tldr.outcome: Clients get complete connection instructions in one extra lookup, apex domains can be aliased, and an HTTPS record also tells a client to use the https scheme.

facts.value: More than eight aliases NOT RECOMMENDED

today: RFC 9460 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2023, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is still the definition of the SVCB and HTTPS record types.

sections.title: The Problem and the Goals
sections.content:
The SVCB ("Service Binding") and HTTPS resource records give clients complete instructions for accessing a service. Today HTTP clients resolve only A and AAAA records, learning IP addresses and nothing more. If a client learned more before connecting, it could upgrade http URLs to https, enable HTTP/3 or Encrypted ClientHello, or switch to a better endpoint.

The records also help when a service operator wants to delegate control to another domain. A CNAME can sometimes do that, but it is inadequate when the operator must provide a bound set of consistent parameters such as network location, protocol and keying information, and it is not allowed at a zone apex.

The design goal is for a client to resolve one additional DNS record that gives alternative endpoints with their own parameters, without assuming that all endpoints have the same capabilities or even the same operator.
sections.eli5: Normally a phone book only gives you a house number. This new entry also says which door to use, what language to speak and who to call if nobody answers.

sections.title: The SVCB Record Format
sections.content:
The SVCB record is RR type 64 and the HTTPS record is RR type 65. Their presentation form is SvcPriority TargetName SvcParams. SvcPriority is a number from 0 to 65535, TargetName is a domain name, and SvcParams is an optional list of key=value pairs.

On the wire, the RDATA is a 2-octet SvcPriority, the uncompressed TargetName, and then the SvcParams. Each parameter has a 2-octet key, a 2-octet length and the value. Keys MUST appear in strictly increasing numeric order with no repeats. A client MUST consider the record malformed if the data ends mid-parameter, the keys are out of order, or a value has the wrong format, and then it MUST reject the whole RRset and fall back to a connection without SVCB.

For a generic SVCB query, the service name gets a label for the scheme prefixed with an underscore, for example _examplescheme.api.example.com.. Such records do not change which name a client authenticates: TLS clients MUST still validate certificates for the original service name.
sections.eli5: Each entry is a small form with a ranking number, the name of the place to go, and a list of notes. The notes have to be written in a fixed order so that everybody reads them the same way.

sections.title: AliasMode and ServiceMode
sections.content:
The SvcPriority value selects the mode. A value of 0 means AliasMode, and anything else means ServiceMode. Within one RRset, all records SHOULD have the same mode, and if an AliasMode record is present the recipient MUST ignore any ServiceMode records.

AliasMode points a service at another name. Its main purpose is aliasing at the zone apex, where CNAME is not allowed. Unlike CNAME, it does not affect other record types and applies only to a specific service. Recipients MUST ignore any SvcParams in an AliasMode record, and clients and resolvers MUST limit how many aliases they follow, though the limit MUST NOT be zero.

ServiceMode describes an alternative endpoint and its connection parameters. A smaller SvcPriority means the domain owner prefers that record, and clients SHOULD randomly shuffle records with equal priority for load balancing. A TargetName of . has a special meaning: in AliasMode it says the service is not available, and in ServiceMode it means the record's owner name is the effective target.
sections.eli5: An alias is a note that says "we moved, go there instead". A service entry says "you can come in this way, and here is how". Lower ranking numbers are the owner's favorites.

sections.title: Client and DNS Server Behavior
sections.content:
A client resolves a service in a loop. It builds the query name, asks for the SVCB record, and if it gets an AliasMode record it repeats the query for the TargetName. If it gets compatible ServiceMode records, it sorts them by ascending SvcPriority and tries them in order, resolving A and AAAA records for the chosen TargetName. This works without any server being aware of SVCB.

Clients for existing protocols such as HTTP are SVCB-optional: they can still connect without ServiceMode records. If the DNS responses are cryptographically protected and SVCB resolution fails, the client SHOULD abandon the attempt, because otherwise an attacker could force a downgrade by denying access to the parameters.

Authoritative servers SHOULD put A, AAAA and SVCB records for in-zone TargetNames in the Additional section, and SVCB-aware recursive resolvers SHOULD chase aliases and add the results there. With a conforming resolver, using SVCB adds no network latency to connection setup. A client MAY start an optimistic connection if address records arrive first, and SHOULD wait 50 milliseconds before doing so.
sections.eli5: The client asks for the sign, follows any "we moved" notes, picks the best door from the list, and finds the street address. Helpful resolvers can hand over the address in the same envelope to save a trip.

sections.title: The Initial Service Parameters
sections.content:
This RFC defines a few parameters for ServiceMode records.

  • alpn and no-default-alpn list the application protocols (ALPN identifiers) the endpoint supports. Each scheme defines a default set, and no-default-alpn removes it. A record with no-default-alpn MUST also have alpn.
  • port gives the TCP or UDP port to use, instead of the authority endpoint's port.
  • ipv4hint and ipv6hint carry IP addresses a client MAY use. If A and AAAA records for the TargetName are locally available, the client SHOULD ignore the hints.
  • mandatory lists keys that a client must understand. A record is "compatible" only if the client recognizes all mandatory keys, and incompatible records are ignored.

Unless a protocol mapping says otherwise, clients MUST ignore any parameter they do not recognize. Unknown keys can be written as keyNNNNN in zone files.
sections.eli5: The notes on the sign cover things like which ways in are supported, which door number to use, a few address hints, and a list of notes you absolutely must understand or else skip that entry.

sections.title: The HTTPS Record
sections.content:
The HTTPS record is an SVCB-compatible type specific to the http and https schemes. Clients MUST NOT perform SVCB queries or accept SVCB responses for those schemes. It uses the same parameters, the default ALPN set is the single value http/1.1, and the automatically mandatory keys are port and no-default-alpn.

For https on port 443 the query name is just the origin's hostname, with no underscore labels. That makes HTTPS records work with wildcards and with existing CNAME chains. Clients still validate TLS certificates against the origin, not the TargetName, and MUST support TLS Server Name Indication.

An HTTPS record also works like HSTS. Before an http request, the client SHOULD look for HTTPS records on the equivalent https URL, and if it finds AliasMode or compatible ServiceMode records, it SHOULD behave as if it received an HTTP 307 redirect to that URL. Compared with Alt-Svc, HTTPS records can be learned without first making an HTTP connection, but they are shared by groups of clients, so they cannot be tailored to a single client.
sections.eli5: The HTTPS version of the sign is for websites. If it exists, your browser knows to use the secure door right away and can even skip straight to the faster modern entrance.

sections.title: Zone Structures and Examples
sections.content:
Section 10 shows how operators lay out their zones. To add HTTP/3 support to a simple site, the owner adds @ 7200 IN HTTPS 1 . alpn=h3, which also tells clients to upgrade http to https. To alias an apex to a hosting pool, one more record does it: @ 7200 IN HTTPS 0 pool.svc.example.. Clients still treat the original names as the origins and validate certificates for them.

Parameters can be bound to each server pool, so a primary pool can offer alpn=h2,h3 while a backup pool offers only h2 on a different port. For performance, domain owners SHOULD minimize AliasMode records and zone structures that need more than eight aliases are NOT RECOMMENDED.

A multi-CDN example shows the risks: a network adversary might force clients onto a CDN that lacks a desired feature, and because A, AAAA and HTTPS lookups are independent they can be answered by different CDNs.
sections.eli5: The examples show real signs: one that says "we also have the fast entrance", one that says "our front door is really that building", and one with different rules for the main and backup buildings.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
SVCB and HTTPS records can travel over untrusted channels, so clients are REQUIRED to verify that the alternative endpoint is authoritative for the service. For that reason DNSSEC signing and validation are OPTIONAL. Clients MUST partition their DNS cache per local network, or flush it on network changes, so a local attacker cannot plant forged records that follow users to other networks.

An attacker who can block SVCB resolution can deny clients the benefits, which is why clients SHOULD abandon the attempt when they detect such an attack. A hostile DNS party might forge an AliasMode record with a TargetName of . to block a particular service, and clients that might be subject to this SHOULD ignore such records. Records can also point at internal addresses and ports, so protocol mappings SHOULD list appropriate port restrictions.

On privacy, SVCB queries reveal the user's intent to use a particular protocol, in addition to the domain. The RFC intends the records to be used over a privacy-preserving DNS transport such as DNS over TLS or DNS over HTTPS.
sections.eli5: Because the sign could be faked, the client still checks that the place it ends up at really is the shop it wanted. It also keeps separate notebooks for each place it has been, so a trick at one cafe cannot follow it home.

items.label: no-default-alpn
items.desc: No support for the default protocol.

data.title: Primary and backup pools
data.code:
$ORIGIN svc.example. ; A hosting provider
pool  7200 IN HTTPS 1 . alpn=h2,h3
              HTTPS 2 backup alpn=h2 port=8443
pool   300 IN A        192.0.2.2
              AAAA     2001:db8::2
backup 300 IN A        192.0.2.3
              AAAA     2001:db8::3
